x-m-e5-01.title: Finding Two Numbers with a Given Greatest Common Factor and Least Common Multiple
x-m-e5-01.goal: Find on your own two numbers that meet the greatest common factor and least common multiple conditions at the same time, and discover the relationship between the conditions.
x-m-e5-01.material: Seoa drew two number cards. Both numbers are natural numbers that are 40 or less. Seoa only said this: "The greatest common factor of the two numbers is 6, and the least common multiple is 36." What are the two numbers? (Say the smaller number first.)
x-m-e5-01.thinking.0: Reading the conditions as relationships of factors and multiples
x-m-e5-01.thinking.1: Finding and checking several examples that meet all the conditions
x-m-e5-01.thinking.2: Guessing a pattern from the examples you found
x-m-e5-01.prereq.0: The meanings of factor and multiple, and of common factor and common multiple (Grade 5, first semester level)
x-m-e5-01.s.s1.prompt: From the statement that the greatest common factor of the two numbers is 6, what must be true about the two numbers?
x-m-e5-01.s.s1.hint.0: Turn 'the two numbers have 6 as a factor' into a statement about dividing the two numbers by 6.
x-m-e5-01.s.s1.hint.1: Write a few numbers related to 6, such as 6, 12, 18, 24, and look at whether 6 is a factor or a multiple of those numbers.
x-m-e5-01.s.s1.r.a: The factors of 6 are only 1, 2, 3, and 6. Think about whether the two numbers could be bigger than 6.
x-m-e5-01.s.s1.r.b: This read 'common factor' as 'a number that divides both with nothing left over,' and thought of it as a relationship between factors and multiples.
x-m-e5-01.s.s1.o.c: At least one of the two numbers is 6
x-m-e5-01.s.s1.r.c: Even if the greatest common factor is 6, both numbers can be bigger than 6. Test with two multiples of 6 that are bigger than 6.
x-m-e5-01.s.s1.o.d: The difference of the two numbers is 6
x-m-e5-01.s.s1.r.d: Pick two multiples of 6 and compare their greatest common factor with their difference. Are they always the same?
x-m-e5-01.s.s1.explain: 6 is a common factor of the two numbers, so both numbers divide evenly by 6. That is, both numbers are multiples of 6. The extra condition, that the greatest common factor must not be greater than 6 while they are multiples of 6, can be tested in the next step.
x-m-e5-01.s.s2.prompt: Find 2 different pairs of two numbers that fit the conditions (smaller number a, larger number b). The larger number is 40 or less.
x-m-e5-01.s.s2.hint.0: Both numbers are multiples of 6, so each can be written as 6 times some natural number. First write out the multiples of 6 that are 40 or less.
x-m-e5-01.s.s2.hint.1: Pair two of them and check whether the least common multiple is 36 and whether the greatest common factor is not greater than 6. If not, change to a different pair.
x-m-e5-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Both numbers must be natural numbers.
x-m-e5-01.s.s2.ok.c2: The smaller number is less than the larger number, and the larger number is 40 or less.
x-m-e5-01.s.s2.fail.c2: Write the smaller number in a and the larger number in b, and make b 40 or less.
x-m-e5-01.s.s2.fail.c3: The greatest common factor of the two numbers is not 6.
x-m-e5-01.s.s2.fail.c4: The least common multiple of the two numbers is not 36.
x-m-e5-01.s.s2.explain: (12, 18) and (6, 36) are all the pairs that fit the conditions. For 12=6×2 and 18=6×3, the numbers you get by dividing the two numbers by 6, 2 and 3, have no common factor besides 1, and 6×2×3=36. 6=6×1 and 36=6×6 work the same way.
x-m-e5-01.s.s3.prompt: For the two pairs you found, find the product of the two numbers each time. How did the products turn out? Is it a coincidence? Also compare with the product of the greatest common factor 6 and the least common multiple 36, and write your guess.
x-m-e5-01.s.s3.hint.1: Also find the product of 6 and 36 and put it side by side with the products above to compare.
x-m-e5-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you calculate again to check that the products you found are really the same for the two pairs?
x-m-e5-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you test your idea about 'Is it a coincidence?' with two other numbers (for example, 4 and 6)?
x-m-e5-01.s.s3.model.0: 12×18=216 and 6×36=216, so the products of the two pairs were the same. The greatest common factor 6 times the least common multiple 36 is also 216, so it doesn't seem to be a coincidence.
x-m-e5-01.s.s3.model.1: If you find the products, 12×18 is 216 and 6×36 is 216. The product of two numbers seems to be the same as (greatest common factor)×(least common multiple), and when I tried 4 and 6, 2×12=24=4×6, so it worked.
x-m-e5-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that even tested with other numbers

x-m-e5-02.title: The Number of Groups to Share Equally: Fixing the Solution
x-m-e5-02.goal: Find and fix the place in a solution where the wrong relationship between numbers (factor/multiple) was chosen, and consider all the cases that fit the conditions.
x-m-e5-02.material: You want to share 48 candies and 36 chocolates equally with none left over among several groups. Hayun found the number of groups like this.
x-m-e5-02.thinking.0: Finding a logic error in a solution
x-m-e5-02.thinking.1: Choosing the relationship between numbers that fits the situation
x-m-e5-02.thinking.2: Finding several values that meet the conditions
x-m-e5-02.prereq.0: The meanings of factor and multiple, and what 'divides evenly' means (Grade 5, first semester level)
x-m-e5-02.s.s1.prompt: Pick one wrong line in Hayun's solution.
x-m-e5-02.s.s1.hint.0: Read each line and think about whether what it says is actually possible in the situation with 48 candies and 36 chocolates.
x-m-e5-02.s.s1.hint.1: If there were 144 groups, think about how many candies one group would get.
x-m-e5-02.s.s1.line.0: We want to share 48 candies and 36 chocolates equally with none left over.
x-m-e5-02.s.s1.line.1: The number of groups must be a multiple of 48 and also a multiple of 36, so we find the common multiples.
x-m-e5-02.s.s1.line.2: The smallest of the common multiples of 48 and 36 is 144.
x-m-e5-02.s.s1.line.3: So we can share among 144 groups.
x-m-e5-02.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is the first wrong place. The number of groups that share 48 equally must be a number that divides 48 evenly, that is, a factor of 48. A multiple can be bigger than 48, and then there are not enough candies. Line 4 also says something that would leave some groups without a single candy with 144 groups. Line 1 copied the problem well, and the 144 in line 3 is correct as the least common multiple of 48 and 36.
x-m-e5-02.s.s2.prompt: Find 3 different numbers of groups (2 groups or more) that you can share among equally with none left over.
x-m-e5-02.s.s2.hint.0: First write down some numbers of groups that can share the 48 candies equally with none left over.
x-m-e5-02.s.s2.hint.1: Check one by one whether the 36 chocolates can also be shared with none left over by that number.
x-m-e5-02.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a natural number that is 2 or more.
x-m-e5-02.s.s2.fail.c1: Make the number of groups a natural number that is 2 or more.
x-m-e5-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The 48 candies can be shared equally with none left over.
x-m-e5-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The 48 candies are left over or not enough.
x-m-e5-02.s.s2.ok.c3: The 36 chocolates can also be shared equally with none left over.
x-m-e5-02.s.s2.fail.c3: The 36 chocolates are left over or not enough.
x-m-e5-02.s.s2.explain: The possible numbers of groups are 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12. The most groups is 12, and then one group gets 4 candies and 3 chocolates.
x-m-e5-02.s.s3.prompt: You want to write a note to Hayun. Write why you should think about factors, not common multiples, using the 48 candies or the 36 chocolates as an example.
x-m-e5-02.s.s3.hint.0: First write how many candies one group would get if you did it Hayun's way.
x-m-e5-02.s.s3.hint.1: Think about whether the number of groups sharing 48 can be bigger than 48.
x-m-e5-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does your number example show why Hayun's solution does not work?
x-m-e5-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say, with a reason, which of 'factor' and 'multiple' fits the situation?
x-m-e5-02.s.s3.model.0: Hayun, the number of groups has to be a number that can share the 48 candies equally with none left over, that is, a factor of 48. With 144 groups there are not enough candies, so you can't give even 1 to a group. So you have to find the common factors of 48 and 36.
x-m-e5-02.s.s3.model.1: The number of groups is the number we divide by, so it has to be a number that divides 48 evenly. A multiple can be bigger than 48, so there would not be enough candies. For example, if you share the 36 chocolates among 40 groups, some groups would get none.

x-m-e5-03.title: Finding the Wrong Answers Without Calculating
x-m-e5-03.goal: Estimate the size of the result of fraction addition to rule out wrong answers, and find several pairs of fractions that make the same sum.
x-m-e5-03.material: Four friends calculated 2/3 + 1/4. Seonu said 3/7, Bora said 5/6, Sian said 1 5/12, and Doyun said 11/12. See whether you can rule out the wrong answers by estimating alone, before calculating.
x-m-e5-03.thinking.0: Setting the range of the result by estimating
x-m-e5-03.thinking.1: Telling apart what an estimate tells you from what it cannot tell you
x-m-e5-03.thinking.2: Finding several pairs that make the same sum
x-m-e5-03.prereq.0: How to compare the sizes of fractions with different denominators (Grade 5, first semester level)
x-m-e5-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the answers you can say are 'wrong' by estimating alone, without calculating exactly.
x-m-e5-03.s.s1.hint.0: If you add a positive number to 2/3, will it be greater or less than 2/3?
x-m-e5-03.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the number you add, 1/4, with 1/3 and think about whether the sum is greater or less than 1.
x-m-e5-03.s.s1.r.a: This considered that the result cannot be smaller than the starting number 2/3.
x-m-e5-03.s.s1.r.b: 5/6 is greater than 2/3 and less than 1, so you cannot say it is wrong by estimating alone. Estimating can rule out wrong answers, but it cannot confirm that the answers left over are right.
x-m-e5-03.s.s1.r.c: This used the fact that 1/4 is less than 1/3 to consider that the sum must be less than 1.
x-m-e5-03.s.s1.r.d: This value is between 2/3 and 1, so estimating does not rule it out. To choose from the remaining candidates you need an exact calculation.
x-m-e5-03.s.s1.explain: You added 1/4 to 2/3, so the sum must be greater than 2/3. So 3/7 (about 0.43) is not possible. Also, 1/4 is less than 1/3, so the sum must be less than 2/3 plus 1/3, that is, 1. So 1 5/12 is not possible either. 5/6 and 11/12 are between 2/3 and 1, so estimating cannot sort them out (the real answer is one of the two).
x-m-e5-03.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 different pairs of two proper fractions that have different denominators and cannot be simplified any further (numerators a and c, denominators b and d, denominators 12 or less) and that add up to 11/12.
x-m-e5-03.s.s2.hint.0: First write the pairs where, with the denominator made 12, some/12 + some/12 = 11/12.
x-m-e5-03.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the pairs you wrote can be rewritten so that no fraction can be simplified and the denominators are different.
x-m-e5-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The numerator must be 1 or more and less than the denominator.
x-m-e5-03.s.s2.ok.c2: All are natural numbers and the denominators are 12 or less.
x-m-e5-03.s.s2.fail.c2: Make all the numbers natural numbers and the denominators 12 or less.
x-m-e5-03.s.s2.ok.c3: Neither fraction can be simplified any further.
x-m-e5-03.s.s2.fail.c3: There is a fraction that can be simplified.
x-m-e5-03.s.s2.fail.c4: The two denominators are the same. Make them different.
x-m-e5-03.s.s2.ok.c5: The sum of the two fractions is 11/12.
x-m-e5-03.s.s2.fail.c5: The sum of the two fractions is not 11/12.
x-m-e5-03.s.s2.explain: For example, 2/3+1/4, 1/2+5/12, 1/3+7/12, 1/6+3/4, and 1/12+5/6 all make 11/12. The same pair written in the other order (for example, 1/4+2/3) counts as the same example.
x-m-e5-03.s.s3.prompt: Seonu said, "You just add the denominators together and the numerators together," and got 2/3+1/4=3/7. Explain to Seonu (1) why it is wrong, using estimation, without calculating, and (2) the correct way to calculate, using common denominators.
x-m-e5-03.s.s3.hint.0: Compare Seonu's answer 3/7 and the starting number 2/3 with a decimal or with 0.5, and see which is bigger.
x-m-e5-03.s.s3.hint.1: Find a number that both denominators 3 and 4 divide evenly, and change the two fractions to the same denominator.
x-m-e5-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does your estimate show why Seonu's answer 3/7 is impossible?
x-m-e5-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is it clear that in the calculation with common denominators you only add the numerators?
x-m-e5-03.s.s3.model.0: Seonu, if you add 1/4 to 2/3 it should be bigger than 2/3, but 3/7 is smaller than 2/3, so it is wrong. When the denominators are different, you make them a common denominator of 12 and add 8/12+3/12=11/12.
x-m-e5-03.s.s3.model.1: 3/7 is less than 0.5, but 2/3 is more than 0.5, so adding can't make the result smaller. You must not add the denominators. Make a common denominator of 12, a common multiple of the denominators 3 and 4, and then add only the numerators.

x-m-e5-04.title: Choosing the Information You Really Need from the Garden Story
x-m-e5-04.goal: Use the relationship between a part shown as a fraction and the whole to judge what information is really needed to find an area.
x-m-e5-04.material: Jiu's family garden will have red peppers on 3/8 of the whole garden and lettuce on 1/4 of it, and eggplants on all the rest. The shape and the area of the garden have not been told yet.
x-m-e5-04.thinking.0: Sorting out the part of the information already given that is enough
x-m-e5-04.thinking.1: Judging what information is needed to change a rate into an actual amount
x-m-e5-04.thinking.2: Seeing that different information can lead to the same answer
x-m-e5-04.prereq.0: That a fraction shows the size of a part compared to the whole (Grade 5 level)
x-m-e5-04.s.s1.prompt: The rest of the garden where eggplants will go is what fraction of the whole garden?
x-m-e5-04.s.s1.hint.0: Change the lettuce part 1/4 into how many eighths.
x-m-e5-04.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what is left if you set the whole as 1 (or 8/8) and take away the part already planted.
x-m-e5-04.s.s1.r.a: This is the size of the pepper part and the lettuce part put together. Think again about what to do with this sum with respect to the whole.
x-m-e5-04.s.s1.r.b: This solved it with the idea of taking the two planted parts away from the whole.
x-m-e5-04.s.s1.r.c: If you subtract 1/4 from 3/8, you get 1/8. But think about what this subtraction compares with what.
x-m-e5-04.s.s1.r.d: This is the value after taking away only the lettuce part. Check where the pepper part went.
x-m-e5-04.s.s1.explain: If you add the pepper part 3/8 and the lettuce part 1/4 (=2/8), you get 5/8, and if you take 5/8 away from the whole 8/8, 3/8 is left.
x-m-e5-04.s.s2.prompt: You want to know the area of the eggplant garden in m². Which of the following, if just one is told to you, lets you find the area of the eggplant garden?
x-m-e5-04.s.s2.hint.0: All you know now is the rates, 'what fraction.' Think about which actual area of one part you would need to change these rates into actual areas.
x-m-e5-04.s.s2.hint.1: Suppose the lettuce part is 8 m². Then how many m² would the whole garden and the eggplant garden each be?
x-m-e5-04.s.s2.r.a: Even with the same perimeter, the area of a rectangle changes depending on its shape. The perimeter alone does not tell you the area of a part.
x-m-e5-04.s.s2.o.b: The area of the lettuce part
x-m-e5-04.s.s2.r.b: This considered that using the relationship that the lettuce part is 1/4 of the whole, you can work back to the area of the whole.
x-m-e5-04.s.s2.o.c: The area needed to plant one pepper plant
x-m-e5-04.s.s2.r.c: If you do not know the number of plants, you cannot know the area of the pepper part. The area of one plant does not tell you the size of the whole garden.
x-m-e5-04.s.s2.o.d: The area of the whole garden
x-m-e5-04.s.s2.r.d: This considered that if you know the area of the whole, you can use the relationship of 3/8 of the whole right away.
x-m-e5-04.s.s2.o.e: The area of the pepper part
x-m-e5-04.s.s2.r.e: This considered that using the relationship that the pepper part is 3/8 of the whole, you can work back to find the area of the whole.
x-m-e5-04.s.s2.explain: You already know what fraction of the whole each part is, so if you know the area of just one of the whole, the pepper part, or the lettuce part, you can find all the other areas. The perimeter or the area one plant needs cannot change these rates into actual areas.
x-m-e5-04.s.s3.prompt: Even if you do not know the area of the pepper part, if you know just the area of the lettuce part, you can find the area of the eggplant garden. Use the example of the lettuce part being 16 m² to explain why.
x-m-e5-04.s.s3.hint.0: First write what fraction of the whole the lettuce part, 16 m², is.
x-m-e5-04.s.s3.hint.1: After you find the area of the whole, use what fraction of the whole the eggplant garden is to find its area.
x-m-e5-04.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If the lettuce part is 16 m², ...
x-m-e5-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you find the whole using the relationship that the lettuce part is 1/4 of the whole?
x-m-e5-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you use that the eggplant garden is 3/8 of the whole to find the final value?
x-m-e5-04.s.s3.model.0: The lettuce part is 1/4 of the whole, so the whole is 16×4=64 m². The eggplant garden is 3/8 of the whole, so it is 3/8 of 64, which is 24 m². If you know the area of one part and how much of the whole it is, you can know the whole.
x-m-e5-04.s.s3.model.1: The lettuce part, 16 m², is one box when the whole is split into 4 boxes, so the whole is 64 m², and if you split it into 8 boxes, one box is 8 m². The eggplant garden is 3 of those boxes, so it is 24 m².

x-m-e5-05.title: A Garden Made with 20 m of Fence: Sorting Out the Areas
x-m-e5-05.goal: Make the possible rectangles yourself for a fixed perimeter, compare their areas, and guess a rule about the shape with the greatest area.
x-m-e5-05.material: Hajun wants to use all 20 m of fence, with none left over, to make a rectangular garden. The length and width are natural numbers (in m). The bigger the garden, the better.
x-m-e5-05.thinking.0: Making several examples that fit the conditions
x-m-e5-05.thinking.1: Judging the possibilities by considering every case
x-m-e5-05.thinking.2: Applying a rule to a new situation
x-m-e5-05.prereq.0: The meanings of perimeter and area of a rectangle (Grade 4 level)
x-m-e5-05.s.s1.prompt: Find 2 rectangular gardens with different shapes that have a perimeter of 20 m and an area of 24 m² or more, giving the length (a) and the width (b). (A length and width swapped count as the same shape.)
x-m-e5-05.s.s1.hint.0: If the perimeter is 20 m, what must the length and width add up to? Once you decide the length, the width is decided.
x-m-e5-05.s.s1.hint.1: Change the length as 1, 2, 3, ... and write (length)×(width) in a table.
x-m-e5-05.s.s1.ok.c1: The length and the width are natural numbers.
x-m-e5-05.s.s1.fail.c1: Make the length and the width natural numbers (1 or more).
x-m-e5-05.s.s1.fail.c2: To use all the fence with none left over, the perimeter must be 20 m.
x-m-e5-05.s.s1.ok.c3: The area is 24 m² or more.
x-m-e5-05.s.s1.fail.c3: The area is less than 24 m².
x-m-e5-05.s.s1.explain: Length + width = 10. If the length is 1 the area is 9, if 2 it is 16, if 3 it is 21, if 4 it is 24, and if 5 it is 25. The only ones that are 24 or more are (4, 6) and (5, 5).
x-m-e5-05.s.s2.prompt: Hajun said, "If I choose the length and width well, I might be able to make a garden with an area of 26 m² or more." When the length and width are natural numbers, how would you best judge this statement?
x-m-e5-05.s.s2.hint.0: Write all the natural numbers the length can be, and find the width and area for each.
x-m-e5-05.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the areas when the length is 6 or more with the earlier cases.
x-m-e5-05.s.s2.o.a: It can be made. If you make the length longer, the area keeps getting bigger
x-m-e5-05.s.s2.r.a: If you make the length longer, the width gets shorter. Check what happens to the area when the length is 6, 7, and 8.
x-m-e5-05.s.s2.o.b: We cannot know. We cannot test all the numbers the length and width could be
x-m-e5-05.s.s2.r.b: The natural numbers the length can be are only 1 through 9. Count to see whether you really cannot test them all.
x-m-e5-05.s.s2.o.c: It cannot be made. If you check all the possible lengths, the area does not go over 25
x-m-e5-05.s.s2.r.c: This judged by listing all the possible cases without missing any and checking them.
x-m-e5-05.s.s2.o.d: It can be made. If you use decimals, you can make 26 too
x-m-e5-05.s.s2.r.d: This problem fixed the numbers as natural numbers, and even if you try with decimals like 5.5×4.5, the area is 24.75, which does not go over 25.
x-m-e5-05.s.s2.explain: With length + width = 10, when the length is 1 to 9, the areas are 9, 16, 21, 24, 25, 24, 21, 16, 9. The biggest value is 25, so 26 or more cannot be made.
x-m-e5-05.s.s3.prompt: Looking at the table, what happens to the area as the difference between the length and the width gets smaller? Apply this rule to a perimeter of 24 m, and guess and write the length and width of the shape that seems to have the greatest area, and that area.
x-m-e5-05.s.s3.hint.0: Look at the length and width in the row of the table with the greatest area.
x-m-e5-05.s.s3.hint.1: If the perimeter is 24 m, first find what the length and width add up to.
x-m-e5-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you draw your guess out of the numbers in the table?
x-m-e5-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you first work out what the length and width add up to for a perimeter of 24 m?
x-m-e5-05.s.s3.model.0: The smaller the difference between the length and width, the bigger the area. With a perimeter of 24 m, length + width = 12, so I think a 6 m × 6 m square, with an area of 36 m², is the greatest.
x-m-e5-05.s.s3.model.1: The more alike the length and width are, the bigger the area, so I think a square is the greatest. With a perimeter of 24, one side is 6 m and the area is 6×6=36 m².

x-m-e5-06.title: What Seems Off in This Parallelogram Area Solution?
x-m-e5-06.goal: Find the mistake in a solution for the area of a parallelogram, evaluate a way to show it is wrong without calculating, and then fix it correctly.
x-m-e5-06.material: Minseo found the area of a parallelogram with a base of 10 cm, a slanted side of 5 cm, and a height of 4 cm like this. (The height is the length measured perpendicular to the base.)
x-m-e5-06.thinking.0: Finding where the error in a solution is
x-m-e5-06.thinking.1: Evaluating a reason that shows it is wrong without calculating
x-m-e5-06.thinking.2: Fixing it correctly and explaining why
x-m-e5-06.prereq.0: The meanings of base and height of a parallelogram, and the area of a rectangle (Grade 5 level)
x-m-e5-06.s.s1.prompt: Pick the first wrong line in Minseo's solution.
x-m-e5-06.s.s1.hint.0: Read each line and see in which line the two new lengths, 5 cm and 4 cm, were used.
x-m-e5-06.s.s1.hint.1: When the parallelogram is changed into a rectangle, say in words which length of the parallelogram the length and the width each equal.
x-m-e5-06.s.s1.line.0: The base of the parallelogram is 10 cm, the slanted side is 5 cm, and the height is 4 cm.
x-m-e5-06.s.s1.line.1: A parallelogram can be changed into a rectangle, so the area is (base)×(slanted side).
x-m-e5-06.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is the wrong place. If you cut a parallelogram and change it into a rectangle, the length becomes the base and the width becomes the 'height.' The slanted side does not become the width. Lines 3 and 4 followed the number sentence in line 2, so the calculation itself is right, but the number sentence is wrong.
x-m-e5-06.s.s2.prompt: What is the best way to show, without calculating anything new, that Minseo's solution (10×5=50) is wrong?
x-m-e5-06.s.s2.hint.0: Keep the base and the slanted side the same length, and imagine the parallelogram lying down more and more.
x-m-e5-06.s.s2.hint.1: Compare whether the area changes while it lies down, and whether the value of 10×5 changes.
x-m-e5-06.s.s2.o.a: 10×5 is the area of a rectangle with a length of 10 cm and a width of 5 cm, so the parallelogram is the same
x-m-e5-06.s.s2.r.a: Even when the base and the slanted side are the same, the shapes can be different. Check whether a rectangle and a parallelogram are the same shape.
x-m-e5-06.s.s2.o.b: The height 4 cm is shorter than the slanted side 5 cm, so the height cannot be used to calculate the area
x-m-e5-06.s.s2.r.b: A length being short does not mean it cannot be used. Think again about what the height shows.
x-m-e5-06.s.s2.o.c: If you keep the slanted side at 5 cm and lay it flatter, the area gets smaller but 10×5 stays the same
x-m-e5-06.s.s2.r.c: By imagining the shape changing while the base and the slanted side stay the same, this showed that the number sentence does not follow the change in the shape.
x-m-e5-06.s.s2.o.d: The area of a parallelogram is always greater than the product of the base and the slanted side
x-m-e5-06.s.s2.r.d: Imagine the shapes yourself and see whether there are cases where the area is greater than the product of the base and the slanted side. When is the greatest case?
x-m-e5-06.s.s2.explain: A parallelogram with a base of 10 cm and a slanted side of 5 cm has the greatest area when it is a rectangle (50 cm²), and the more you lay it down, the flatter it gets and the smaller the area. But 10×5 does not change, so this number sentence cannot be the area of a parallelogram.
x-m-e5-06.s.s3.prompt: Fix Minseo's solution correctly, and explain why the slanted side 5 cm was not needed.
x-m-e5-06.s.s3.hint.0: First find the area using the base and the height.
x-m-e5-06.s.s3.hint.1: Explain in words which length becomes the width when you change it into a rectangle.
x-m-e5-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The area is ... cm². This is because ...
x-m-e5-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is your corrected number sentence one that multiplies the base and the height?
x-m-e5-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you connect why the slanted side is not needed to the idea of changing into a rectangle?
x-m-e5-06.s.s3.model.0: 10×4=40, so the area is 40 cm². The area of a parallelogram is the base times the height, so we don't use the slanted side, 5 cm.
x-m-e5-06.s.s3.model.1: The area is 40 cm². If you cut and paste a parallelogram to make a rectangle, the length is the base, 10 cm, and the width is the height, 4 cm, so the slanted side is not needed.

x-m-e5-07.title: If the Averages Are the Same, Are the Two Groups Alike?
x-m-e5-07.goal: Check, with data and an example you make yourself, that even when averages are the same, how spread out the data is can be different, and tell apart what an average tells you from what it cannot tell you.
x-m-e5-07.material: The Sky group and the Sea group each sent 4 people to a jump rope contest. The Sky group's records (number of jumps) are 20, 22, 24, and 54, and the Sea group's records are 28, 29, 30, and 33. The averages of both groups are the same, 30. Doha said, "The averages are the same, so the two groups are equally good."
x-m-e5-07.thinking.0: Checking the reason for a claim against the data
x-m-e5-07.thinking.1: Writing out the meaning of average with a sum and a count
x-m-e5-07.thinking.2: Making data that meets conditions yourself
x-m-e5-07.thinking.3: Saying the limits of an average
x-m-e5-07.prereq.0: The meaning of average (a value that evens out the data), and that you add up all the data values and divide by the count (Grade 5 level)
x-m-e5-07.s.s1.prompt: From the fact that the averages of the two groups are the same, what can you say for sure? Check each choice against the records above.
x-m-e5-07.s.s1.hint.0: For each choice, check one by one whether it is true for the records of the Sky group and the Sea group.
x-m-e5-07.s.s1.hint.1: Remember how an average is found (what you add and what you divide by) and think backward.
x-m-e5-07.s.s1.o.a: The highest records of the two groups are the same
x-m-e5-07.s.s1.r.a: The Sky group's highest record is 54 and the Sea group's is 33. An average does not tell you the biggest value.
x-m-e5-07.s.s1.o.b: The totals of the records of the two groups are the same
x-m-e5-07.s.s1.r.b: This read the process of finding an average backward and thought of the total as (average)×(number of people).
x-m-e5-07.s.s1.o.c: The lowest records of the two groups are the same
x-m-e5-07.s.s1.r.c: The Sky group's is 20 and the Sea group's is 28. Even if averages are the same, the smallest value can be different.
x-m-e5-07.s.s1.o.d: The records of both groups are gathered about equally close together
x-m-e5-07.s.s1.r.d: The Sky group is spread out from 20 to 54, and the Sea group is gathered from 28 to 33.
x-m-e5-07.s.s1.explain: An average is (total of everything)÷(number of people), so if the number of people is the same and the averages are the same, the totals are the same too (both are 120). But you cannot say that the biggest value, the smallest value, and how spread out they are are the same.
x-m-e5-07.s.s2.prompt: Make new records for a group of 4 people with an average of 30. Write the records from smallest as a ≤ b ≤ c ≤ d, and make 2 different groups in which the difference between the person with the most jumps and the person with the fewest (d−a) is 20 or more.
x-m-e5-07.s.s2.hint.0: First decide what the records must add up to when the average is 30 and there are 4 people.
x-m-e5-07.s.s2.hint.1: Make the smallest record a small and the biggest record d big, then fit the sum with the two middle records.
x-m-e5-07.s.s2.ok.c1: The records are natural numbers that are 0 or more.
x-m-e5-07.s.s2.fail.c1: Make the records natural numbers that are 0 or more.
x-m-e5-07.s.s2.ok.c2: They are in order from smallest.
x-m-e5-07.s.s2.fail.c2: Write them in the order a ≤ b ≤ c ≤ d.
x-m-e5-07.s.s2.ok.c3: The four records add up to 120, so the average is 30.
x-m-e5-07.s.s2.fail.c3: The average is not 30. Check the sum of the four records.
x-m-e5-07.s.s2.ok.c4: The difference between the most jumps and the fewest jumps is 20 or more.
x-m-e5-07.s.s2.fail.c4: The difference between the two records is less than 20. Try spreading them out more.
x-m-e5-07.s.s2.explain: For the average to be 30, the four records must add up to 120. Even if the sum is 120, the records can be gathered in one place or spread far apart.
x-m-e5-07.s.s3.prompt: You have to pick just one group as the school's representatives. Which of the Sky group and the Sea group, which have the same average, would you pick? Either is fine. Using the numbers in the records as your reasons, also write what you cannot tell from the average alone.
x-m-e5-07.s.s3.hint.0: Write the smallest and biggest records of the two groups side by side and compare them.
x-m-e5-07.s.s3.hint.1: First decide the purpose of choosing representatives (steady records, big records, and so on) and pick the group that fits it.
x-m-e5-07.s.s3.placeholder: Example: I would pick the ... group. This is because ...
x-m-e5-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Do the numbers you used really show what the group is like?
x-m-e5-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write why the averages being the same does not lead to 'they are equally good'?
x-m-e5-07.s.s3.model.0: I would pick the Sea group. The averages are the same, 30, but the Sea group's records are even, from 28 to 33, and the Sky group's average went up because of one person who jumped over 54.
x-m-e5-07.s.s3.model.1: I would pick the Sky group. Even with the same average, the Sky group has a person who jumped over 54, so it can make a big record. But I have to know that there is also a person as low as about 20, so the records differ a lot.

x-m-e5-08.title: Sorting Out When the Word 'Fifty-Fifty' Fits
x-m-e5-08.goal: Sort out, with reasons, the cases where saying 'the chance is fifty-fifty' fits and the cases where it does not, and make a bag of marbles that fits the conditions yourself.
x-m-e5-08.material: 'The chance is fifty-fifty' means that the chance of something happening and the chance of it not happening are about the same. Friends said "It's fifty-fifty" in several situations.
x-m-e5-08.thinking.0: Telling apart the number of cases from how likely it is to happen
x-m-e5-08.thinking.1: Judging whether an earlier result affects the next result
x-m-e5-08.thinking.2: Making examples that fit conditions for chance
x-m-e5-08.prereq.0: Showing the chance of something happening with words like 'impossible,' 'fifty-fifty,' and 'certain,' or with numbers (Grade 5, second semester level)
x-m-e5-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the cases where the word 'fifty-fifty' fits.
x-m-e5-08.s.s1.hint.0: For each situation, write all the cases that can happen, and think about whether those cases can happen to the same degree.
x-m-e5-08.s.s1.hint.1: Count the number of cases where it happens and where it does not happen, and compare them. If it is a situation you cannot count, also think about why you cannot count it.
x-m-e5-08.s.s1.o.a: You roll a die with faces 1 to 6 once, and an even number comes up
x-m-e5-08.s.s1.r.a: This counted how many of the 6 possible faces are even, and compared the cases where it happens with the cases where it does not.
x-m-e5-08.s.s1.o.b: Tomorrow it either rains or does not rain, one of the two, so it rains
x-m-e5-08.s.s1.r.b: Just because there are only two cases, it does not mean the two cases happen to the same degree. It depends on the weather conditions.
x-m-e5-08.s.s1.o.c: From a bag with 10 marbles, 1 blue marble and 9 red marbles, you take out one marble and a blue marble comes out
x-m-e5-08.s.s1.r.c: There are two colors, but the numbers of marbles are different. Think about whether the chance of a blue marble coming out is the same as the chance of a red marble coming out.
x-m-e5-08.s.s1.o.d: From a bag with 5 red marbles and 5 blue marbles, you take out one marble and a blue marble comes out
x-m-e5-08.s.s1.r.d: This was based on counting the marbles and seeing that the numbers of the two colors are the same.
x-m-e5-08.s.s1.o.e: You flip a fair coin and heads came up 3 times in a row. Heads comes up next
x-m-e5-08.s.s1.r.e: You know that results that came up earlier do not affect the next flip.
x-m-e5-08.s.s1.explain: Of the 6 faces of the die, 2, 4, and 6, three of them, are even, so the cases where it happens and where it does not happen are the same, 3 each. 5 red and 5 blue are also about the same. With a fair coin, earlier results do not affect the next result, so the chances of heads and tails are still the same. Rain and no rain, and 1 blue versus 9 red, do not happen to the same degree even though there are only two cases.
x-m-e5-08.s.s2.prompt: Make a bag with 12 marbles. There are r red, p blue, and y yellow marbles. When you take out one marble, (1) the chance of red is higher than the chance of blue or yellow, (2) blue and yellow can also come out, and (3) the chance of red is not 'fifty-fifty.' Make 3 different bags.
x-m-e5-08.s.s2.hint.0: First decide the number of red marbles. Think about what chance you get if there are 6 red marbles.
x-m-e5-08.s.s2.hint.1: Split the remaining marbles into blue and yellow, making both fewer than the red and at least 1 each.
x-m-e5-08.s.s2.ok.c1: All three colors have at least 1 marble.
x-m-e5-08.s.s2.fail.c1: Make all three colors natural numbers that are at least 1.
x-m-e5-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The marbles must add up to 12.
x-m-e5-08.s.s2.ok.c3: There are more red than blue and yellow.
x-m-e5-08.s.s2.fail.c3: There must be more red than blue or yellow.
x-m-e5-08.s.s2.ok.c4: Red is not half of the total.
x-m-e5-08.s.s2.fail.c4: If there are 6 red marbles, the chance is fifty-fifty. Make it different.
x-m-e5-08.s.s2.explain: There are cases where red is 5, which is less than half but more than blue and yellow, and when it is 7 or more, it is more than half. There are many bags that meet the conditions.

x-m-e5-09.title: Colored Paper Joined Together: Changing Your Mind
x-m-e5-09.goal: Check and fix your guess of a pattern each time more data comes, and explain the correspondence between the number of overlaps and the number of sheets.
x-m-e5-09.material: You want to join sheets of colored paper 10 cm long in a row. Each two neighboring sheets overlap by 2 cm.
x-m-e5-09.thinking.1: Checking and fixing your guess with new data
x-m-e5-09.thinking.2: Applying a correspondence to a new situation
x-m-e5-09.prereq.0: Experience making a table and looking at changes, and adding, subtracting, and multiplying natural numbers (Grade 5 level)
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.prompt: Data comes out one piece at a time. Each time, choose the idea that fits.
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.hint.0: Make a table of the total length for 1, 2, and 3 sheets, and also write how many places overlap.
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.hint.1: Check in the table how much the length changes each time one sheet is added.
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.st.0.info: The length of 1 sheet of colored paper is 10 cm, and if you join 2 sheets the total length is 18 cm.
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.st.0.ask: How long is the total length when 3 sheets are joined?
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.st.0.after: 2 sheets → 18 cm is 10+10−2. With 3 sheets there are two pairs of neighbors, so there are 2 places that overlap, and 30−4=26 cm. Each time you add one more sheet, it gets longer by 10−2=8 cm.
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.st.0.o.a: 28 cm (subtract the overlapping 2 cm just once from the 30 cm length of 3 sheets)
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Count how many places overlap. With 3 sheets, how many pairs of neighboring sheets are there?
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This did not subtract the overlapping parts. Think again about why it was 18 cm for 2 sheets.
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.st.0.o.c: 26 cm (each time one more sheet is added, it gets longer by the same length)
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This considered that the 8 cm increase with 2 sheets repeats each time one more sheet is added.
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.st.1.info: If you join 4 sheets, it is 34 cm. So far: 1 sheet is 10 cm, 2 sheets is 18 cm, 3 sheets is 26 cm, 4 sheets is 34 cm.
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.st.1.ask: What pattern fits all the data so far?
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.st.1.after: In the table the length goes up by 8 each time, and with 1 sheet it is 10 cm, so it is 8×1+2. This pattern also fits 4 sheets (8×4+2=34). You have to check a pattern against all the data, not just one piece of data.
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This checked one by one by plugging in that it fits all the data from 1 sheet through 4 sheets.
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.st.1.r.b: With 1 sheet it would be 8 cm, which is different from the data. It fits only for 2 sheets; check how it is for the others.
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.st.1.r.c: With 1 sheet it would be 18 cm, which is different from the data (10 cm).
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.st.2.info: When joining 20 sheets, Somi said "20×10−2=198 cm," and Hajun said "20×10−2×19=162 cm."
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.st.2.after: The number of places that overlap is (number of sheets−1), so Hajun's number sentence is right, and it is 162 cm, the same as 8×20+2.
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Somi. There is only one place that overlaps
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Think back to how many places overlapped with 3 sheets.
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Hajun. The number of places that overlap is 19, one fewer than the number of sheets
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This drew from the earlier data that the number of sheets and the number of overlapping places are different.
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Both are wrong. With 20 sheets it is 20×8=160 cm
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The 2 is missing from 8×20. Check whether the length would be 8 when there is 1 sheet.
x-m-e5-09.s.s1.reflect: At first you calculated looking only at the number of sheets. Where did you change your thinking? How are the 'number of sheets' and the 'number of overlapping places' different?
x-m-e5-09.s.s2.prompt: To make a strip longer than 100 cm with this colored paper, at least how many sheets do you have to join? Also write how you found out.
x-m-e5-09.s.s2.hint.0: Using the pattern you found, find the lengths for 10, 12, and 13 sheets.
x-m-e5-09.s.s2.hint.1: To find the number of sheets that first goes over 100 cm, also check the length for the number of sheets just before it.
x-m-e5-09.s.s2.placeholder: Example: ... sheets are needed. This is because ...
x-m-e5-09.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you check the lengths for both 12 sheets and 13 sheets and compare them with 100 cm?
x-m-e5-09.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Does the pattern you used fit the earlier data (1 sheet to 4 sheets)?
x-m-e5-09.s.s2.model.0: 13 sheets are needed. With 12 sheets it is 8×12+2=98 cm, which falls short of 100 cm, and with 13 sheets it becomes 106 cm.
x-m-e5-09.s.s2.model.1: Each time one more sheet is added, it gets longer by 8 cm, and 12 sheets is 98 cm and 13 sheets is 106 cm, so at least 13 sheets are needed.

x-m-e5-10.title: Finding the Correspondence in a Row of Matchstick Squares
x-m-e5-10.goal: Find the correspondence between two quantities in a table, make values that are not in the table yourself to check that the pattern is right, and use the pattern to solve a problem.
x-m-e5-10.material: You make squares joined in a row with matchsticks. A side that touches the next square uses one matchstick shared by both. 4 matchsticks are needed for 1 square, 7 for 2 squares, and 10 for 3 squares.
x-m-e5-10.thinking.0: Finding the correspondence in a table
x-m-e5-10.thinking.1: Making new examples with a pattern
x-m-e5-10.thinking.2: Applying a pattern to a problem
x-m-e5-10.thinking.3: Explaining why the pattern is the way it is
x-m-e5-10.prereq.0: Experience making a table and looking at changes, and adding and multiplying natural numbers (Grade 5 level)
x-m-e5-10.s.s1.prompt: Write the number of matchsticks m needed to make n squares for 3 different values of n that are 5 or more and not in the table.
x-m-e5-10.s.s1.hint.0: Make a table of how much the number of matchsticks goes up for 1 square, 2 squares, and 3 squares.
x-m-e5-10.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the amount it goes up each time you join one more is always the same, and use that number to keep writing on until 5 squares.
x-m-e5-10.s.s1.fail.c1: For a value not in the table, make the number of squares a natural number that is 5 or more.
x-m-e5-10.s.s1.ok.c2: The number of matchsticks needed fits the pattern.
x-m-e5-10.s.s1.fail.c2: The number of matchsticks needed does not fit the pattern. Look again at the values for 1, 2, and 3 squares.
x-m-e5-10.s.s1.explain: Each time a square is added, the matchsticks go up by 3. The first square is 4, and 3 more is added each time one is joined, so with n squares it is 3×n+1.
x-m-e5-10.s.s2.prompt: You have 100 matchsticks. What is the greatest number of squares you can make in a row? (It is okay if some matchsticks are left over.)
x-m-e5-10.s.s2.hint.0: Using the pattern you found, find the number of matchsticks needed when n=30 and compare it with 100.
x-m-e5-10.s.s2.hint.1: Make n a little bigger each time and find when the number of matchsticks needed first goes over 100.
x-m-e5-10.s.s2.r.a: This considered that each square uses 4 matchsticks. Think again about whether there are sides that are shared when they are joined.
x-m-e5-10.s.s2.r.b: This used the pattern backward to find the greatest number of squares that does not need more than 100 matchsticks.
x-m-e5-10.s.s2.r.c: Check how many matchsticks 34 squares needs by the pattern.
x-m-e5-10.s.s2.r.d: Check how many matchsticks are left over after making 32 squares, and whether you can join one more square with them.
x-m-e5-10.s.s2.explain: With n squares you need 3×n+1 matchsticks. With n=33, 3×33+1=100, which fits exactly, and with n=34 you need 103, which is not enough. With 32 squares you use 97 and have 3 left over, and with 3 you can join one more square.
x-m-e5-10.s.s3.prompt: Explain the pattern between the number of squares and the number of matchsticks in words, and write why it is not 'number of squares × 4.'
x-m-e5-10.s.s3.hint.0: In the table, picture the shape of two squares joined and think about why 2 squares do not make 4×2=8 matchsticks.
x-m-e5-10.s.s3.hint.1: Count how many new sides you have to place when you add one more square.
x-m-e5-10.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Each time a square is added, ...
x-m-e5-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the pattern you wrote fit starting from 1 square (4 matchsticks)?
x-m-e5-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did 'the reason you must not multiply by 4' connect to the sides that touch?
x-m-e5-10.s.s3.model.0: Each time one more square is added, the matchsticks go up by 3. So you can multiply the number of squares by 3 and add 1. You don't multiply by 4 because a side that touches the next square uses a matchstick together.
x-m-e5-10.s.s3.model.1: Start from 4 at first, and each time you join a square, add 3. Each square does not need 4 because sides that are joined overlap.
